title: How would you estimate how many piano tuners work in Chicago?
description: A step-by-step estimate for "How many piano tuners work in Chicago?" with the approach, the maths and a sanity check.
hook: Chicago has roughly 70 full-time piano tuners: about 70,000 tunings a year, divided by about 1,000 tunings one tuner can do. The question is usually credited to the physicist Enrico Fermi, and it is still the cleanest test of whether you can turn a vague question into a chain of sensible guesses. Have a go yourself before reading on.
body:
The question

How many piano tuners work in Chicago?

Before any numbers, pin down two things. First, the area: the city of Chicago (about 2.7M people) or the wider metro area (more than 9M). Second, the unit: people who call themselves piano tuners, or full-time equivalents. Many tuners work part time or also repair and restore instruments, so full-time equivalents are the cleaner thing to estimate. Say so:

"I'll take the city of Chicago and estimate full-time-equivalent tuners. I'll size the demand for tunings, then divide by what one tuner can do in a year."

The approach: demand divided by capacity

You cannot count tuners directly, but you can count the work they do. That gives a two-part structure:

  • Demand: pianos in the city × tunings each piano gets per year.
  • Capacity: tunings one tuner can complete per year.

Split pianos into homes and institutions (schools, churches, universities, concert halls, bars and studios). Institutional pianos are played harder and tuned more often, so lumping them in with home pianos would understate demand. This is the same demand-over-capacity logic you use for hairdressers in London or dentists in the UK.

Step by step

1. Home pianos

  1. People in Chicago: 2.7M (a round figure; recent Census estimates are just above this).
  2. ÷ 2.5 people per household = 1.08M households.
  3. × 5% of households with a piano = 54,000 home pianos. Pianos are expensive and bulky, and many city flats have no room for one, so 1 in 20 feels reasonable.
  4. × 1 tuning per year = 54,000 tunings. Tuners recommend once or twice a year; many home pianos are neglected for years. Once a year is a fair average.

2. Institutional pianos

  1. Assume 8,000 pianos in schools, churches, colleges, venues and studios. This is a guess, so build it and say so: assume about 4,000 schools, churches, colleges and venues with two pianos each on average.
  2. × 2 tunings per year = 16,000 tunings.

3. Total demand and capacity

LinePianosTunings a year
Homes54,00054,000
Institutions8,00016,000
Total62,00070,000

One tuning takes about an hour and a half, plus travel across the city. So a tuner manages about 4 tunings a day × 250 working days = 1,000 tunings a year.

70,000 ÷ 1,000 = about 70 full-time-equivalent piano tuners.

Sanity check from a second angle

Per head. 2.7M people ÷ 70 tuners is about one tuner for every 39,000 people. A tuner is a rare trade, so one per few tens of thousands of people sounds right; one per 1,000 or one per million would not.

Against official data. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics counted about 350 employed "musical instrument repairers and tuners" in the Chicago metro area in May 2023 (BLS occupational employment data). The city holds a bit under a third of the metro population, which points to roughly 100 people. That category covers every instrument, not just pianos, and it leaves out the self-employed, and many piano tuners work for themselves. So it does not give you the answer, but it confirms the order of magnitude: tens of tuners, not thousands.

Which assumption matters most?

Two inputs drive the answer: the share of households with a piano and the tunings one tuner can do. Test them out loud:

  • If 10% of households owned a piano, home tunings double to 108,000 and the answer rises to about 124.
  • If tuners average 3 tunings a day rather than 4, capacity falls to 750 a year and the answer rises to about 93.

Saying this shows the interviewer you know where the estimate is fragile, which is worth more than a precise number.

What a strong answer sounds like

"I estimate about 70 full-time tuners. That comes from roughly 70,000 tunings a year, three quarters of them home pianos, divided by about 1,000 tunings per tuner. The number I'm least sure of is piano ownership: at 10% of homes it would be closer to 120. If you were a piano retailer thinking about offering tuning, I'd treat this as a small, fragmented trade of a few dozen independents."

A weak answer jumps straight to "maybe 200?" with no structure, or multiplies the full population by a piano share, skipping households and so overstating pianos by 2.5x.

Common mistakes

  • Counting people, not homes. Pianos belong to households. Use households, or you inflate the answer by the household size.
  • Forgetting institutions. Schools and churches add almost a quarter of the demand here.
  • Assuming a tuner tunes eight hours a day. Travel, repairs and admin eat into capacity. Allow for it.
  • Stopping at the number. End with what it means: a small, local, owner-operated trade.

Practise it

Work these out before opening the answers.

1. Suppose tuners spend a quarter of their working time on repairs. How many full-time equivalents are needed now?

Show the answer

Tuning capacity falls to 75% of 1,000 = 750 tunings a year. 70,000 ÷ 750 = about 93 tuners. Every bit of non-tuning work raises the number of people needed.

2. At $150 per tuning, how big is the Chicago tuning market, and what does one tuner earn in revenue?

Show the answer

70,000 × $150 = $10.5M a year. Per tuner: 1,000 × $150 = $150k of revenue, before travel, tools and the gaps between jobs. That looks like a decent living for a full-time tuner, which suggests the assumptions hang together.

3. The interviewer says only 2% of Chicago homes have a piano. What is your new answer?

Show the answer

Home pianos: 1.08M × 2% = 21,600, so 21,600 tunings. Add 16,000 institutional tunings for 37,600 in total. 37,600 ÷ 1,000 = about 38 tuners. Institutions now make up over 40% of demand, so you would want to check that 8,000 figure next.
